summary: Mill Valley sits in a canyon at the base of Mount Tamalpais, and its entire 4.9 square miles are threaded with redwood-shaded creeks and steep hillside roads that dead-end into open space — a geography that makes the town feel substantially more remote than a place seven miles north of the Golden Gate Bridge has any right to feel. That proximity to San Francisco defines the commute calculus: Highway 101 and the Golden Gate Transit bus lines funnel workers south, making this firmly a bedroom community rather than a job center, with a median household income of $208,466 reflecting the Bay Area professional salaries earned elsewhere. The affordability math, though, is stark — median home values exceed $2 million, yielding a price-to-income ratio above 9.5:1, and even median rent of $3,313 per month claims roughly 19% of that high gross income. The compact downtown, anchored along Miller Avenue and stretching toward a small central plaza, supports independent restaurants, bookshops, and coffee spots that give the town a distinct identity rather than a franchised-strip feel. Annual daytime highs average a mild 65°F with nearly nine hours of daily sunshine, though summer fog rolling over the Tam ridgeline can drop temperatures sharply by evening. Trails from town climb directly into Mount Tamalpais State Park and the Muir Woods watershed without a car. The defining tension is spatial: the same canyon walls and protected parkland that make Mill Valley strikingly beautiful also cap housing supply permanently, so the cost of entry tracks upward against a geography that cannot expand.
